```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Evaluated wherever INLA and the serving stack are installed (CI and
# development machines); rendered as static code elsewhere.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  eval     = all(vapply(
    c("INLA", "vetiver", "pins", "plumber", "callr", "httr2", "yardstick"),
    requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE
  ))
)
```

inlaops registers six S3 methods against the `"bru"` class so that
`vetiver_model()` works with inlabru fits out of the box — the same way it
works with `lm()` or `mgcv::gam()`. This vignette walks through the full
workflow: fitting, pinning, serving over HTTP, and monitoring.

## Prerequisites

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(inlabru)
library(vetiver)
library(pins)
library(plumber)
library(inlaops)
```

## 1. Fit a model

Always set `config = TRUE` so that the fit stores the posterior
configurations needed for sampling at the `/predict` endpoint.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
n   <- 200
dat <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(n),
  x2 = rnorm(n)
)
dat$y <- 2 + 0.8 * dat$x1 - 0.4 * dat$x2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)

fit <- bru(
  y ~ Intercept(1) + x1 + x2,
  family  = "gaussian",
  data    = dat,
  options = bru_options(
    control.compute = list(config = TRUE, dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE)
  )
)
```

## 2. Wrap with vetiver

`vetiver_model()` dispatches on the `"bru"` class. inlaops provides the
description, metadata, and input prototype (the predictor columns a
request must carry) automatically.

The prediction formula goes into the pin metadata as a **character
string** — R expressions do not survive the YAML metadata round-trip. The
API parses it once when it starts. Training-time fit criteria (WAIC, DIC)
can ride along for monitoring later.

```{r}
v <- vetiver_model(
  fit, "gaussian_glm",
  metadata = list(
    pred_formula = "~ Intercept + x1 + x2",
    n_samples    = 200L,   # posterior samples per request; 200 is the default
    waic         = fit$waic$waic,
    dic          = fit$dic$dic
  )
)
v
v$prototype
```

### Aside — parsnip-fitted models

If you fit via `parsnip::fit()` instead of `inlabru::bru()` directly, pass
the inner bru fit to `vetiver_model()`. The bridge does not auto-unwrap
parsnip's `model_fit`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit_p <- bru_reg(family = "gaussian") |>
  parsnip::set_engine("inlabru") |>
  parsnip::fit(y ~ Intercept(1) + x1 + x2, data = dat)

v_parsnip <- vetiver_model(
  fit_p$fit, "gaussian_glm",   # note: fit_p$fit
  metadata = list(pred_formula = "~ Intercept + x1 + x2")
)
```

## 3. Pin to a versioned board

```{r}
board <- board_temp()   # swap for board_s3(), board_connect(), etc.
vetiver_pin_write(board, v)

pin_versions(board, "gaussian_glm")
```

## 4. Serve the API and call it

In production the API runs on its own (see `vignette("docker")`). Locally
you would run this in a separate R session; it blocks until stopped:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pr() |>
  vetiver_api(v) |>
  pr_run(port = 8088)
```

To keep this vignette self-contained we start the same API in a
background R process instead. It reads the model back from the pin
board, as a deployed API would:

```{r}
port <- httpuv::randomPort()

server <- callr::r_bg(
  function(board_path, port) {
    library(inlaops)
    v <- vetiver::vetiver_pin_read(pins::board_folder(board_path), "gaussian_glm")
    plumber::pr() |> vetiver::vetiver_api(v) |> plumber::pr_run(port = port)
  },
  args = list(board_path = board$path, port = port)
)

# Wait until the API answers its health check.
for (i in 1:60) {
  up <- tryCatch(
    {
      httr2::request(sprintf("http://127.0.0.1:%d/ping", port)) |>
        httr2::req_perform()
      TRUE
    },
    error = function(e) FALSE
  )
  if (up || !server$is_alive()) break
  Sys.sleep(1)
}
stopifnot(up)
```

Any HTTP client can now ask for predictions. From R, vetiver's own client
sends a data frame and returns a tibble:

```{r}
endpoint <- vetiver_endpoint(sprintf("http://127.0.0.1:%d/predict", port))

new_obs <- data.frame(x1 = c(0.5, -1.2), x2 = c(1.0, 0.3))
predict(endpoint, new_obs)
```

The response carries the posterior mean (`.pred`), the 2.5th and 97.5th
posterior quantiles (`.pred_low`, `.pred_high`), and the posterior
standard deviation (`.pred_sd`) — not just a point estimate, so
downstream consumers can propagate predictive uncertainty. The true
means here are 2 + 0.8 x1 − 0.4 x2: 2.0 and 0.92.

Callers outside R send the same rows as JSON:

```sh
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8088/predict \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '[{"x1": 0.5, "x2": 1.0}, {"x1": -1.2, "x2": 0.3}]'
```

Requests are checked against the input prototype, so a body missing a
predictor column is rejected:

```{r}
try(predict(endpoint, data.frame(x1 = 0.5)))
```

```{r}
server$kill()
```

For packaging the model into a container, see `vignette("docker")`.

## 5. Track model quality across versions

INLA-specific fit metrics (WAIC, DIC) cannot be recomputed from a live
endpoint — they are only available at training time. They were stored as
pin metadata above; read them back per version for longitudinal
monitoring:

```{r}
versions <- pin_versions(board, "gaussian_glm")

do.call(rbind, lapply(versions$version, function(ver) {
  meta <- pin_meta(board, "gaussian_glm", version = ver)
  data.frame(version = ver, waic = meta$user$waic, dic = meta$user$dic)
}))
```

Standard prediction-drift monitoring uses `vetiver_compute_metrics()`
against the `.pred` column, the same as any other vetiver model. Drift
monitoring is time-windowed, so the input data needs a timestamp column.
In a real deployment this comes from the time you collected each
observation — here we synthesise one:

```{r}
monitoring_data <- dat  # in production: observations collected since deployment
monitoring_data$.pred <- inlabru::generate(
  fit, newdata = monitoring_data,
  formula = ~ Intercept + x1 + x2, n.samples = 500
) |> rowMeans()

# Synthetic timestamps for the example. Replace with real collection times.
monitoring_data$obs_date <- seq.Date(
  from       = as.Date("2026-01-01"),
  by         = "day",
  length.out = nrow(monitoring_data)
)

metrics_board <- board_temp()

new_metrics <- vetiver_compute_metrics(
  monitoring_data,
  date_var = obs_date,
  period   = "week",
  truth    = y,
  estimate = .pred
)

# vetiver_pin_metrics() appends to an existing metrics pin — the first time
# you record metrics, write the pin directly with pins::pin_write(). On
# subsequent runs (e.g. weekly cron jobs), use vetiver_pin_metrics() so each
# new window's rows are appended without overwriting history.
if ("gaussian_glm_metrics" %in% pins::pin_list(metrics_board)) {
  vetiver_pin_metrics(metrics_board, new_metrics, "gaussian_glm_metrics")
} else {
  pins::pin_write(metrics_board, new_metrics, "gaussian_glm_metrics")
}

head(pins::pin_read(metrics_board, "gaussian_glm_metrics"))
```

`period` is the rolling window — `"day"`, `"week"`, `"month"`, etc. Pick
the cadence that matches how often new observations arrive in production.
`vetiver_plot_metrics()` draws the pinned metrics over time.

## Pins board options

| Board | Use case |
|---|---|
| `board_temp()` / `board_folder()` | Local development and testing |
| `board_s3()` | AWS-hosted teams |
| `board_azure()` | Azure-hosted teams |
| `board_connect()` | Posit Connect |

## Multi-likelihood models

The input prototype comes from the **first** likelihood's data, and the
API predicts from that likelihood. For models with multiple `bru_obs()`
calls, supply the prototype manually via `save_prototype`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
v <- vetiver_model(
  fit,
  "multi_lhood_model",
  save_prototype = tibble::tibble(x1 = 0, x2 = 0)
)
```
